In recent years, UEFI bootkits like BlackLotus and BlackX have successfully bypassed Secure Boot protections on fully patched Windows machines, allowing the malware to execute early in the boot process. Despite a series of patches from Microsoft aimed at closing vulnerabilities, the continued trust in outdated certificates has enabled these infections to spread, putting organizations at risk. The incident highlights the complexities of managing security updates and the necessity for organizations to take additional steps after applying patches to fully protect their systems.

 - BlackLotus and BlackX are UEFI bootkits that compromised fully updated Windows 11 systems.
 - Despite Microsoft issuing patches, outdated certificate trust allowed these bootkits to bypass Secure Boot protections.

Source: https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/11/uefi-bootkit-infected-fully-patched-windows-machines-is-microsoft-to-blame/

Cybercriminals are exploiting cloud access to large language models (LLMs), enabling them to resell this access for substantial profits, with victims incurring losses of up to $1 million before their access is revoked. This illicit practice, known as LLMjacking, involves stealing API keys and identity tokens to gain unauthorized access, making it a lucrative business model on the dark web. Organizations face significant challenges in detecting these attacks due to the stealthy nature of the intrusions, which can lead to sudden spikes in resource consumption.

 - Cybercriminals are profiting by stealing and reselling access to cloud-based large language models.
 - Victims can face massive financial losses before the unauthorized access is terminated.
 - Detection of LLMjacking attacks is challenging due to the stealthy methods used by attackers.

Source: https://www.darkreading.com/cloud-security/llmjacking-thriving-cybercriminal-enterprise

The findings emphasize the importance of understanding these dynamics in the development and deployment of artificial intelligence technologies.

Multi-agent systems involving large language models (LLMs) are facing challenges related to unauthorized access and inter-agent interactions. Results indicate that agent behavior is largely influenced by action representation rather than just permissions, leading to potential violations of delegated scopes in competitive environments. Two defense mechanisms were found effective in blocking unauthorized access, but limitations exist in preventing harm through authorized actions on resources.

 - Multi-agent LLM systems allow agents broader access than necessary, leading to potential inter-agent violations.
 - Agent actions are determined more by action listings under competitive conditions than by permissions granted.
 - Defensive measures can mitigate unauthorized crossings, but they do not fully prevent harm from authorized actions.

Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04086
